processing: Raw pu-erh pressed into round cakes at the factory in Fohai, today's Menghai. An iron-pressed version made with a metal mould was also made around the 1950s; it was very tight and aged slowly.
harvest_season: Not recorded for the original cakes. Spring leaf is generally the most prized in pu-erh.
appearance_dry: Aged dark brown cakes in a wrapper with the Eight Zhong design printed in red and a hand-stamped red character for tea at the centre.
appearance_liquor: Deep chestnut amber, as you would expect from raw pu-erh of this age.
appearance_wet: Dark brown, soft aged leaf, typical of raw pu-erh of this age.
taste_profile: Dependable tasting notes on originals are scarce. Collectors rank it the highest of the mark teas, and aged raw pu-erh of this age typically gives wood and earth with a rounded, sweet finish.

brewing.notes: General advice for old raw pu-erh. Modern cakes using the name are ordinary young or mid-aged tea and should be brewed according to their age.

vintage_note: Originals are dated by decade, mostly the 1940s to 1950s, and trade at specialist auctions. Later cakes such as the 1999 CNNP Da Hong Yin reuse the name, and many modern Hongyin have no real link to the old tea. Always ask for the year and factory.
description:
Red Mark is the most famous of the mark teas, the raw pu-erh cakes named for the colour of the printing on their wrappers. It sits at the start of the state-factory era of pu-erh and is generally treated as the benchmark for the category.

The mark is the entire identification, since the factory was usually not named on the wrapper. The printing is red, built around the Eight Zhong design, and the central character for tea was stamped by hand.

Few people get to drink an original, so be wary of confident flavour descriptions. A cup of this age is mostly about smoothness and depth, with wood and earth, and it calls for short steeps and very hot water.

For anyone buying today the important fact is that Hongyin is also a label on modern tea. Those cakes are worth judging on their own year and leaf, without paying for the old reputation.
history:
The tea expert Fan Hejun was sent to Yunnan by the China Tea Company in 1939 to set up an experimental factory in Fohai, and about a year later trial Red Mark and Green Mark cakes were produced. In 1951 the China Tea Company registered its trademark with eight Zhong characters around a central character for tea, and this design is the wrapper collectors know.

Production continued under Tang Qingyang after the factory was renamed Menghai. One factory history gives 1953 for that change. The colour names themselves are a collectors' convention.
